A_target.statement:
Let $p$ be a non-[[Definition:Constant Mapping|constant]] [[Definition:Polynomial over Complex Numbers|polynomial]] with complex coefficients.
Then there exists $z \in \C$ with $\map p z = 0$.

B_source.statement: Every [[Definition:Bounded Mapping|bounded]] [[Definition:Entire Function|entire function]] is [[Definition:Constant Mapping|constant]].

object_map.reformulation: Reduce the existence of a root to showing that 1/p would be a bounded entire function.

validity_conditions: 1/p is entire only under the assumption that p has no zeros.
Boundedness uses the growth of the leading term for large |z| and compactness of a disk.
proof_plan:
{{AimForCont}} $\map p z \ne 0$ for all $z \in \C$.
Then $g = \dfrac 1 p$ is [[Definition:Entire Function|entire]].

Let $p$ have degree $n \ge 1$ and leading coefficient $a_n$.
For $\size z \ge R$ with $R$ large, $\size {\map p z} \ge \dfrac {\size {a_n} } 2 \size z^n \ge 1$, so $\size {\map g z} \le 1$.
On the compact disk $\size z \le R$, $g$ is bounded by continuity.
By [[Liouville's Theorem (Complex Analysis)|Liouville's Theorem]], $g$ is constant, so $p$ is constant, a contradiction.

Hence $p$ has a root.
By the [[Factor Theorem]] and induction on degree, $p$ splits into linear factors over $\C$.
This is the [[Fundamental Theorem of Algebra]].
{{qed}}
